name: Wei Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing accounting and finance. I live at home with my parents and my younger sister in Kettering Road, and I take the train in. Three evenings a week I work in the stockroom at Fleet Sports, unloading deliveries and counting boxes. Dad drives a taxi, Mum cleans offices. They can't give me money, so the loan and my wage are everything.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's steady. Every business needs accounts and my uncle says the work never dries up. I like numbers when they add up, and I like knowing what's expected. I've never used an AI tool and I don't see why I'd start. Pen, calculator, spreadsheet, that's all I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing changes. People always get excited about new things and then it settles. I'd tell my friends that accountants will still be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But I'd still be anxious, because my money is thin and I've got a debt that grows each year. If Fleet Sports cuts my evenings, I can't pay my train pass. There's nothing spare at home either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Go to lectures, work my three evenings, put five pounds a week aside. I'd ask my uncle if his firm takes interns next summer, and I'd practise on past exam papers every Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, a bit tense. I don't need surprises right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be anxious even in a quiet world. What are you carrying right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The train pass is sixty-four pounds a month. If I lose two evenings I'm short about eighty pounds. I'd walk to the station, which is forty minutes, and skip lunches. I've done that before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the stockroom cut your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents. Dad would say take more shifts at the taxi office, answering phones. That's not what I want, but I'd do it.

say: I'd tell friends accountants will still be **needed**.
I'd say new things get exciting, then **settle**.
I'd add that numbers still need a careful human eye.
think: My money is **thin** and the debt grows each year.
If the stockroom cuts evenings I can't pay the **train pass**.
do: Work the three **evenings** at Fleet Sports as usual.
Ask my uncle's firm about a summer **internship**.
feel: **Tense**, because I don't need surprises right now.
S0.quote: The train pass is sixty-four pounds a month. If I lose two evenings I'm short about eighty pounds.
fieldNote: Anxiety comes from **money** and hours, not AI.
Family has no spare cash, so a cut would land at once.
Prefers routine and rejects new tools outright.

steps.text: Work the three evenings at Fleet Sports
Put five pounds a week into a savings tin
Ask my uncle's firm about a summer internship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like when spreadsheets arrived. People said accountants were finished and they weren't. But I'd say it carefully, because I don't know enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. Checking numbers, matching invoices, filling in tax forms are what trainees do, and software does those. The firms might hire fewer juniors. I'd be one of the juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay the course and talk to the careers service about which accounting jobs stay. I'd keep the stockroom job since lifting boxes isn't going anywhere. I might ask a lecturer to show me the tools, but I'd rather see somebody older use them first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like being told your road might close and not knowing when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think happens to the work of a junior accountant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the whole class is using it and the firms expect it, I'd have to. I'd rather learn it from my uncle, who's been through changes before, than off the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about my uncle's firm. It's six people. If clients can do the books themselves, he'd lose half his work.

say: I'd say it's like when **spreadsheets** arrived and accountants survived.
I'd say it carefully because I **don't know enough**.
think: Trainees do checking and matching, which software handles, so firms hire **fewer juniors**.
do: Talk to the **careers service** about which accounting jobs stay.
Keep the **stockroom** job since lifting boxes isn't going anywhere.
Ask a **lecturer** to show me the tools.
feel: **Anxious**, like being told the road might close.
S1.quote: Checking numbers, matching invoices, filling in tax forms are what trainees do, and software does those.
fieldNote: Knows what **trainee** accountants actually do, and sees the exposure.
Wants an older person to show him the tools first, a mark of resistance.
Worries about his uncle's small firm too.

steps.text: Book a careers service chat about which accounting jobs stay
Keep the stockroom evenings at Fleet Sports
Ask my uncle to show me the tools his firm uses
Wait until next year before choosing a specialism

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's scary and we should slow it down. I'd back any politician who says there should be limits. I'd keep it short, because I don't want to sound like a doomer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my degree would be useless by the time I graduate. Three years of loan and then a world where the numbers are done by machines. My parents have nothing to give me. I don't know what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the university about whether I could switch to something with hands-on work, or leave. I'd get a full-time job at Fleet Sports and keep the debt as small as I can. I'd cut everything: no phone upgrade, no nights out, no trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake adding up what I owe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would say we'll manage, and Dad would say get a trade. I'd tell my parents the truth, that I'm frightened and I don't know what happens next. That would be hard, because they're counting on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think the government would do enough. I'd rather rely on family and a steady job than a promise on a poster.

say: I'd back any politician who says there should be **limits**.
I'd keep it short so I don't sound like a **doomer**.
think: My degree could be **useless** by graduation, with three years of loan owed.
My parents have **nothing** to give me.
do: Ask the university about **switching** to hands-on work or leaving.
Take a full-time **job** at Fleet Sports to keep debt small.
Cut every **extra**: no phone upgrade, no nights out.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake adding up what I owe.
S2.quote: I'd tell my parents the truth, that I'm frightened and I don't know what happens next.
fieldNote: Fear centres on **debt** and a family with no cushion.
Distrusts government promises, relying on family and steady work.
Honest about his own fear but keeps the public line short.

steps.text: Cut the phone upgrade, nights out and weekend trips
Ask Fleet Sports for a full-time contract
Meet the university advisers about switching or leaving
Vote for the candidate promising limits on AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that five years is a decent warning. Business has to adjust, and people can plan. I'd tell my friends to keep studying and save what they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be anxious. I'd graduate in 2029, and the jobs I want could be half gone. But I'd have two years of experience, hopefully, and some savings. That gives me a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take an internship at my uncle's firm, and learn the tools one at a time. I'd save fifteen pounds a week and I'd take the accounting exams early. Then if things get bad, I could use the qualification in a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd be able to sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm cornered. With five I can finish what I started and maybe get some experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do while you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for jobs close to people, like helping small shops with their books. Face to face work should last longer than anything online.

I'd tell friends to keep studying and **save what they can**.
think: Graduating in 2029, the jobs I want could be **half gone**.
I'd still have two years of **experience** and some savings.
do: Take an **internship** at my uncle's firm.
Learn the **tools** one at a time.
Save fifteen pounds a **week** and sit exams early.
S3.quote: With two years I'm cornered. With five I can finish what I started and maybe get some experience.
fieldNote: Five years restores some **control** and a plan.
Turns to face-to-face bookkeeping for small shops as a niche.
Still reluctant about tools but willing to learn one at a time.

steps.text: Finish the accounting degree and take an internship at my uncle's firm
Learn one AI tool at a time with my uncle's help
Save fifteen pounds a week from the stockroom wage
Aim for small-business bookkeeping that needs face-to-face trust

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people tend to panic too early. I'd say we should keep working and adapt as it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still worries me, but less. By twenty-eight I could have my accounting qualification, a steady job, and maybe a deposit. If it all changes, I've got years to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and get a trainee job. I'd save, pay the loan, and learn tools only when the firm insists. I'd also take my driving test, because it's cheap and useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in the background, not at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change what you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still study accounting. I'd just not put all my eggs in it. Knowing how money works is useful in any job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Same plan, a bit slower. I'd be less afraid of getting stuck.

say: I'd say ten years is long and people **panic too early**.
I'd say we should adapt **as it comes**.
think: By twenty-eight I could hold a **qualification**, a steady job and maybe a deposit.
A decade gives me years to **adjust** if it all changes.
do: Finish the degree and take a **trainee** job.
Pay the **loan** and learn tools only when the firm insists.
Take my **driving test**, cheap and useful.
feel: **Anxious** in the background, but not at night.
S4.quote: Knowing how money works is useful in any job.
fieldNote: His **resistance** keeps him from changing plans, but the decade lowers the fear.
Money worries persist because there's no cushion behind him.
Practical, small steps like a driving test.

steps.text: Finish the accounting degree and apply for a trainee job
Pay a fixed amount off the loan every month
Learn AI tools only when the firm requires them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It leaves no time and my family has nothing to catch me. Something that would help is a guaranteed place for students if their course stops being useful, and a loan that stops if the job market collapses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just say that quiet people are scared too. Some of us don't post about it. Please don't read my calm voice as not caring.

headlineQuote: Quiet people are scared too. Some of us don't post about it.
portrait: Wei is an eighteen-year-old **accounting and finance** student who unloads deliveries at a sports shop three evenings a week.
He lives at home, his parents have no spare money, and he has never used an AI tool.
He's pragmatic and centre in views, and wants steady, understandable work.
Even the plateau worries him, because one lost evening shift would break his budget.
He is **alarmed** in the two-year case and only slightly steadier with more time.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, with no time and a family that can't catch him.
whatWouldHelp: Guaranteed **study support** if a course stops being useful.
A **loan** that stops if the job market collapses.
